title: The stopping days
hook: Friday prayers, Shabbat, Sunday, Buddhist observance days: many traditions stop work on purpose

segments.voice: Yesterday, Epictetus's two lists, and a job on the outside one. Your line was what was lost was held, not who you are. What did you name about yourself that has nothing to do with work? Today, the days when work stops on purpose. Day nine hundred fourteen.
screen: `WHAT WAS LOST WAS HELD, NOT WHO YOU ARE.`

segments.voice: A Friday at midday, and a shopkeeper pulls down the shutter and walks toward the mosque. A Friday at sunset, and a family lights candles and the phones go into a drawer. A Sunday morning, and church bells over quiet streets. A full-moon day, and a woman in white walks to a Buddhist temple to keep extra precepts until the next morning. Different calendars, different reasons. But each of these is a stopping, chosen on purpose and kept together. Today: the stopping days.
screen: `A SHUTTER, CANDLES, BELLS, WHITE.` → `DIFFERENT CALENDARS.` → `STOPPING ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: Each tradition stops in its own way, so let's take them one at a time. First, Shabbat. The Ten Commandments in Exodus say, "Six days shalt thou labour, and do all thy work: But the seventh day is the sabbath of the LORD thy God: in it thou shalt not do any work." Then the verse keeps going: not you, nor your son or daughter, nor your servants, nor your animals, nor the stranger within your gates. The rest is for everyone in the household, including those who work for you. Shabbat runs from Friday sunset to Saturday nightfall. Second, Friday in Islam. The Qur'an tells believers, when the call to the Friday congregational prayer is heard, to hurry to the remembrance of God and leave their trading; and when the prayer is done, to go out and seek God's bounty again. So Friday is not a full day off in the way Shabbat is. It's a stopping in the middle of the day, for prayer together. Third, Sunday. The book of Revelation speaks of being "in the Spirit on the Lord's day," and Christian tradition came to read the Lord's day as Sunday, the day of the resurrection. Some Christians keep it as a day of rest; others gather and then go about the day; and some, such as Seventh-day Adventists, keep the seventh day, Saturday. Fourth, Buddhist observance days, called uposatha. In the Anguttara Nikaya, the Buddha teaches lay followers to keep extra precepts on these days, for a night and a day following the example of the awakened ones. These days don't ask for the same thing. What they share is a refusal to let work fill every hour.
screen: `SHABBAT: REST FOR EVERYONE.` · `FRIDAY: LEAVE YOUR TRADING.` · `SUNDAY: THE LORD'S DAY.` · `UPOSATHA: EXTRA PRECEPTS.` · then, large: `THE STOPPING DAYS.`

segments.voice: Practice the stop. Let your hands fall still. If something in you is still working, planning, answering, let it hear the shutter come down. Breathe. Then, gently, look ahead at your week. Is there an afternoon, an evening, a morning, that could become a stopping time, kept on purpose? Don't schedule it yet. Just find it, and imagine the quiet in it. The bell holds the time.
The stopping days. Shabbat, the Friday prayer, the Lord's day, the uposatha: times traditions set apart from work on purpose, each in its own way. Today's word.
Your line: the stopping days. Today, plan a stopping time for this week: a day, or part of one, with work put away. Tell someone, so it's kept together. Day nine hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: Shabbat runs from Friday sunset to Saturday nightfall; Muslims gather for the Friday congregational prayer at midday; Christians commonly gather on Sunday, and some keep it as a day of rest; Buddhist lay followers may keep extra precepts on uposatha days.

fork.setup: it's Friday, and the call to the congregational prayer is heard while you're in the middle of selling something. by the Qur'an's verses, what do you do?
options: finish the sale, then pray alone later.
leave the trading and go to the prayer, then return to work after.
close the shop for the whole day.
fork.reveal: the verses say to hurry to the remembrance of God and leave trading, and when the prayer is done, to go out and seek God's bounty.

trapdoor: what you thought: weekends are just time off.
what it means: traditions set apart days, or parts of days, to stop work on purpose and turn toward God or practice.
what a scholar hears: Exodus extending rest to servants, animals and the stranger, the Qur'an's midday Friday stop, the Lord's day in Revelation, and the Buddha's uposatha precepts for laypeople.

notes: Qur'an 62:9–10 is paraphrased (no Pickthall quotation, as the exact wording wasn't verified). A Muslim Keeper should confirm the framing that Friday is a midday stop for congregational prayer rather than a full day of rest.
Shabbat times (Friday sunset to Saturday nightfall) are standard practice but not stated in Exodus; a Jewish reviewer should confirm.
'Christians came to gather on Sunday, the day of the resurrection' is not stated in Revelation 1:10 itself; check framing. Seventh-day Adventists are named as an example of Saturday observance.

Uposatha: AN 8.41 describes laypeople keeping eight precepts on the observance day. The hook's 'full-moon day' and 'woman in white' are illustrative of Theravada practice; a Buddhist Keeper should confirm. The word 'uposatha' is Pali; original is null to avoid guessing a script.
Index hook says 'many traditions'; the script names four and avoids the count claim.

Editor: Sunday-as-Lord's-day now attributed to Christian tradition (not in Revelation 1:10); uposatha line follows AN 8.41 (the awakened ones, not monks or nuns); dropped the repeated 'if you pray' line and varied the practice opener.
